title: Shipping the X thread publishing loop
dek: How a publish journal and automatic rollback turned a fragile sequence of posts into one schedulable content item.
body:
A scheduled post has one obvious success condition: it publishes. A thread has several chances to fail. Every reply has to publish in order, each new post depends on the one before it, and a failure halfway through can leave a broken fragment live on X.

That failure case kept thread publishing out of my content workflow. I could draft a thread, but publishing still meant being present, posting each part by hand, and cleaning up manually if the platform rejected one. Scheduling the first post did not solve the sequence.

The thread publishing loop now treats the whole sequence as one content item. I can draft two to seven parts, review them together, approve them once, and schedule one publication time. When that time arrives, the scheduler publishes the opening post and chains each reply to the post before it.

## Recording what happened

The important part is the publish journal. After each successful post, the scheduler records the platform ID and its place in the sequence. That creates an exact account of how far the thread got instead of reducing the result to a vague success or failure flag.

If the third post fails, the journal still knows that the first two are live. A retry can work from recorded state, and the operator can see which step failed. The system does not have to guess or restart blindly.

This record also makes cleanup possible. When a later reply fails, the scheduler attempts to delete the posts already published in that attempt. It works backwards through the sequence so a partial thread does not remain public as if it were complete. If cleanup itself fails, the attempt record preserves the remaining post IDs for manual recovery.

Rollback matters because social publishing crosses a boundary I do not control. X can accept one request and reject the next. Connections drop. Rate limits move. A reliable workflow has to account for partial success, not only the clean path.

## What it enables

I can now plan a multi-part build-in-public update as one piece of content. The draft, approval, schedule, publish attempt, retry, and cleanup all belong to the same item. I no longer need a separate checklist to keep seven independent posts in order.

That opens a useful format for work that needs more room than a single post: a design decision, an end-to-end shipping note, or a short explanation of what failed and what changed. The extra space only helps when each part earns its place, so the workflow caps threads at seven posts and keeps the same 280-character limit for every part.

The first version is deliberately narrow. It does not promise that an external platform will always cooperate. It records each result, contains partial failures where it can, and leaves enough evidence to recover where it cannot.

The next test is editorial and operational: whether scheduled threads let me publish more complete accounts of the work without losing the specificity that made the strongest one-post updates useful. The publishing loop is ready for that test.
